comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Half of this card is answered directly: `./dev --ssh` now ends by saying the devenv container is still up on port 2222, that it is left up deliberately, that `./dev --perf` reads slow against its baseline while it runs, and how to stop it. The measurement on this card - `frame.decode` at 1.67 ns/byte with the container up against 1.44 with it stopped - is what makes that worth saying at the point it matters rather than in a doc.

The other half turned out differently than this card assumed. It reads "`frame.decode` now sits close enough to its 2.00x tolerance that ordinary machine load crosses it, which means the baseline was recorded on a quieter machine than the one anybody runs this on". Measured on a_28wKty65Z: the baseline still describes this machine. Eight consecutive runs of an unchanged tree at a load average of about ten sat within 1.14x of it for every arithmetic benchmark, `frame.decode` among them at 0.79-0.83 against a baseline of 0.83.

So the fix is not a re-recorded baseline. It is the two things now in place: `--perf` refuses to judge above a one-minute load average of the performance-core count, and the run says what the machine was doing while it measured. The container being up is one of the things that pushes a machine over that line, which is why the tier now names it on the way out.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
Running `./dev --ssh` and then `./dev --perf` reports a regression that is not one. The ssh tier leaves its devenv containers running, and `frame.decode` measures 1.67 ns/byte against a 0.83 baseline with them up and 1.44 with them stopped - so the obvious thing to do, running the out-of-gate tiers in sequence, produces a false failure.

Two things behind it. The containers are left running deliberately, since a devenv is a thing you keep; nothing says so at the point where it matters. And `frame.decode` now sits close enough to its 2.00x tolerance that ordinary machine load crosses it, which means the baseline was recorded on a quieter machine than the one anybody runs this on.

A perf tier that fails for reasons unrelated to the code is one people learn to skip, which costs more than the regression it was built to catch. Worth deciding between: measuring load and refusing to judge when the machine is busy, re-recording the baseline against a realistic machine, or having the ssh tier say what it left running.
title: 📉 The perf tier fails if you ran the ssh tier first
